newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. Thruway outlines $1.5 bln construction plan.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. Thruway outlines $1.5 bln construction plan.

text.p: The New York Thruway Authority chairman on Thursday proposed spending $1.5 billion over six years to repair the state's roads, bridges and canals, but promised that raising tolls would be a "last resort."

Howard Stenberg, who outlined the preliminary plan to the Assembly Transportation Committee in Buffalo, said that only one-third of the program's costs could be funded with existing resources, leaving the gap to be met with tolls and bonds.

If approved, the capital plan, which would spend about 85 percent of the money on roads and bridges and around 15 percent on canals, would create nearly 18,000 jobs and give the economy a $2.3 billion boost, the chairman estimated.
He warned that delaying the improvements by two years would increase their cost by $213 million.

Steinberg said, in making his case for a new six-year plan, that failing to put such a program in place would allow pavements to erode rapidly, while the percentage of deficient bridges would rise 62 percent.
The Authority expects to finalize its plans, as well as its funding proposals, over the several months.

Steinberg made it plain how much he believes is at stake in ensuring the system is well-maintained. "The 1987 collapse of Schoharie Creek Bridge with the tragic loss of ten lives serves as a constant reminder of the need for vigilance."
In justifying the program's scope, the chairman noted that the costs of doing business have risen sharply since 1998, when Thruway rates last were raised.
The Authority gets no state tax dollars and must rely upon tolls to maintain, run and police the system, and pay for statutory mandates.
Out-of-state drivers pay about one-third of the tolls the Thruway collects, Steinberg said in prepared remarks, noting the system's fatality rate is half the national average.

The Authority also highlighted its steps to cut costs, including eliminating 267 positions and leaving 250 unfilled, replacing toll collectors with the E-ZPass electronic system, and not giving non-unionized employees raises this year.

"No one, including me, likes to pay tolls, but people understand that it costs money to maintain the roads and bridges and the fairest system is to have the people who drive pay for them," Steinberg added.
The list that follows provides a brief breakdown of how the Authority proposed spending the $1.5 billion.
--$770 million to rehabilitate 250 bridges, including $132 million for the Tappan Zee Bridge.
--$382 million to repair 814 lane miles of highway.
--$182 million for capital needs for the canals.
--$160 million for heavy equipment, the electronic toll program, and maintenance for buildings and toll booths.
--$47 million for economic development projects mandated by statute.
